note: Sources: her quantization lecture is the recording transcribed in course/L13.transcript.md (it opens "for this lecture, we will cover large language model quantizations"); course/L12.transcript.md is the serving lecture, and the slide markers in both transcripts point at the other PDF. Slides: course/L12.txt / L12.pdf.
beats: Hook: GPTQ squeezed a 175-billion-parameter model to 3 or 4 bits in a few hours, and it ran faster on fewer GPUs (3-bit OPT-175B on one 80 GB A100 instead of five: check) (line_gptq_cards_packed).

Why not just retrain? Fine-tuning a 175B model to repair the rounding is out of reach, so: one-shot post-training quantization from a small calibration set (128-512 samples); larger models are easier to quantize (slides 19-20; line_grow, line_gptq_tailor_fittings).

GPTQ's idea (slide 21): round a few weights, then nudge the not-yet-rounded ones to cancel the error, left to right, like pinning a hem and smoothing the rest before the next pin (line_gptq_tailor_pin_hem). H = 2XX^T says which neighbours move together: intuition only.
Old way vs GPTQ: picking the easiest weight next meant recomputing H and its inverse after every weight: months; a fixed order plus one Cholesky factorisation: hours (line_gptq_tailor_two_ways).
Results (slide 22): 3-bit OPT-175B, per-token latency at batch 1 3.24x (A100) / 4.53x (A6000) lower (check); small groups rescue 2-bit (taped slide 22).

Kernels (slide 23): the INT4-to-FP16 unpacking from L12-02 has to be nearly free: AutoGPTQ, ExLlama, Marlin, inside vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM (line_gptq_unpack_relay; line_quant_vacuum_unpack from L12-02).

AWQ (slide 24): only about 1% of the weights matter a lot: the ones that meet big activations, found by watching real inputs (line_awq_worn_path); scale those channels up before rounding and the activation down, so they round more precisely (line_awq_bubble_wrap).
Results (slide 25): INT4 with groups of 128 matches FP16 on MBPP and GSM8K; about 3x faster than FP16 at batch 1 (check).
llama.cpp (slide 26): plain C/C++, CPU and Apple silicon first: run the model at home, privately (line_local_laptop_elephant); GGUF uses small blocks (16-32) that a CPU can afford.

k-quants (slide 27): different layers get different bits, 2-6, like packing a suitcase item by item (line_kquant_suitcase_mix). Takeaway: careful rounding beats retraining: fix one and adjust the rest (GPTQ), or protect the few that matter (AWQ).
Cover (line_cover_l12_03; for the X post and thumbnails, not a film beat): the tailor pins a coat hem from left to right, smoothing the loose fabric ahead of each pin.

drawings.prompt: The tailor (the same character in every picture): an invented older tailor with a simple round face, dot eyes, small round glasses, short curly hair, a cloth tape measure draped around the neck, a cardigan over a shirt with rolled-up sleeves, and a round pincushion strapped to the left wrist.
